articles.title: 12TB of Steam Files Leak as a Decade’s Worth of First- and Third-Party Game Data Is Exposed
articles.summary: Approximately 12TB of data has been reportedly extracted from Steam, which apparently encompasses everything that was published on the platform between 2003 and 2013. According to Valve-related content creator Gabe Follower, the data has allegedly been gathered via a publicly accessible endpoint…
body: Gabe Follower notes this data includes the entire Steam library from the period between 2003 and 2013 – not just Valve games. The 12TB of data is said to contain both complete games and beta versions of games, and a variety of early and unseen prototype versions of games that were placed on Steam sometime within that 10-year period have already been uncovered by archivists, enthusiasts, and other interested parties. For instance, those digging have found a build of Left 4 Dead from several months prior to its actual release which features a different HUD, voice lines which never featured in the retail version, and sections of the map that were subsequently altered.
With the sheer size of the leaked data pile, it’s likely more such information will be revealed as people search through it.
Luke is a Senior Editor on the IGN reviews team. You can track him down on Bluesky @mrlukereilly to ask him things about stuff.

articles.title: Halloween: The Game Gets Denied a Rating in Yet Another Country
articles.summary: It's not only fans in Australia who will have to sit on the sidelines and watch others play Halloween: The Game when it launches on Sept. 9. In Japan, Halloween: The Game won't be available on PlayStation, as it has been denied a rating from the Computer Entertainment Rating Organization (CERO)…
body: For a game to launch in Japan, it needs a domestic rating from CERO. If CERO refuses to rate a game, companies will have to work around this and instead try to obtain a rating from the International Age Rating Coalition (IARC), which makes it possible for games to be sold digitally when CERO denies a rating. However, even that option won't make Halloween: The Game available for PS5 users in Japan.

Thanks to its IARC rating, Halloween: The Game will be available on Xbox and PC. Regarding the PlayStation release, in March 2022, Sony changed its policies so the PS Store in Japan would accept IARC-rated games. However, CERO ratings were still required for physical releases or for digital releases rated 18+. Since Halloween has been deemed a mature game in Japan due to its "visceral violence and nudity," it requires a CERO rating in order to launch on the PS Store.

articles.title: New Pokémon Movie Announced After 7 years, and It Will Be the First of Its Kind
articles.summary: Pokémon is getting ready to answer the question of whether its massively successful trading card game would still exist in a world where Pokémon are real, and it will do so with the franchise's first theatrical movie in seven years.
body: The trailer shared during the convention shows a boy described as a " Pokémon TCG player" alongside a Mimikyu, followed by a glimpse of a table set up for a game of Pokémon. The movie will be animated by CloverWorks ( Spy x Family, The Elusive Samurai ), directed by Katsuhiko Kitada ( Evangelion: 2.0 You Can (Not) Advance ), with character design by Akemi Hayashi ( Banana Fish ).

Pokémon: Wild Card will be the 25th movie in the franchise (including 2019's live-action Detective Pikachu ), and the first to follow 2020's Pokémon the Movie: Secrets of the Jungle. This will also be the first animated movie not to feature longtime anime protagonist Ash/Satoshi, and to focus on the Pokémon TCG. Until now, all the Pokémon movies have been treated more or less as spin-offs of the anime, but with the conclusion of the original series in 2023, it seems that the franchise is finally moving in a different direction.

articles.title: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 beta Steam numbers haven't budged in the second weekend, despite Warzone's arrival and transformative patch
articles.summary: We're deep in the second and final session of the Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 beta. This open portion is available on one more platform - Switch 2, and can be accessed without the need for a pre-order.
body: The beta's peak concurrent player count of 115,145, which was achieved over the first weekend, has yet to be beaten. The closest it has got was a little over 113,000 on Friday, likely due to player interest in Warzone. Of course, it's always worth keeping in mind that we have no visibility on PlayStation 5, Xbox or Switch 2 numbers - it's possible some or all of those platforms saw big turnouts in the second weekend.
All that said, Steam is often a good barometer for the performance of most major games, and it's notable that despite the new stuff and the beta's free accessibility, the numbers didn't improve.
Beyond simply comparing and contrasting numbers, there's also the matter of the key gameplay changes Infinity Ward introduced to the beta this session to address the most popular points of feedback.

articles.title: 1666: Amsterdam's developer says it 'won't be using AI anymore', and the tech was only used 'in conception and pre-production'—arguably the most creative phase of the entire process
articles.summary: There was surprise and delight when Summer Game Fest brought the reveal of 1666: Amsterdam, the long awaited dream project from Assassin's Creed co-creator Patrice Désilets.
body: Désilets' studio Panache Digital Games copped to using AI in the production of certain assets, then apologised and promised to remove those elements in time for the early access launch. With that launch happening last week, Désilets now says that Panache has decoupled AI from its pipeline entirely and it won't be using AI in future.

Speaking to GamesRadar+, Désilets stressed that Panache was done with generative AI, and claimed that most of the AI used occurred in the early stages of the project. "Yes, we use some AI in the process, mostly at the beginning," Désilets explained. "In conception and pre-production. It's been totally removed and we won't be using it anymore."

As someone who likes their art made by, y'know, artists, I'm glad that Panache has done what it can to scrape generative AI out of 1666: Amsterdam. That said, it irks me when developers say they only used AI at the concepting stage of development, because that's the most fun and rewarding part of any creative project.
points: There was surprise and delight when Summer Game Fest brought the reveal of 1666: Amsterdam, the long awaited dream project from Assassin's Creed co-creator Patrice Désilets.

articles.title: The Expanse: Osiris Reborn Looks Like the Best Video Game Adaptation Ever
articles.summary: You can’t jump in The Expanse: Osiris Reborn, the upcoming third-person shooter set in James S.A. Corey’s expansive universe of interplanetary politics.
body: There’s precedent here: You can’t jump in the original Mass Effect trilogy, the games to which Osiris Reborn is frequently (and rightfully) compared. But there’s also a lore implication; most scenes in The Expanse are set in spaceships, on space stations, or at lunar ports with variable gravity. Its characters regularly wear magnetized boots so as to stick to the ground. Jumping? Not exactly recommended.

To be clear, this rationale does not come directly from developer Owlcat Games. At Gamescom 2026, I recently played 90 minutes of a mid-game level of The Expanse: Osiris Reborn. A producer watching along would not officially confirm or deny series lore as the reason why you can’t jump in the game. But it nevertheless struck me (hi, big fan of the show) as a small detail showing Owlcat is creating what could be one of the most faithful gaming adaptations ever.

articles.title: HBO Just Officially Introduced a Notorious Batman Villain to the DC Universe
articles.summary: John Stewart (Aaron Pierre) has already spent two months training to become a Green Lantern when HBO’s Lanterns begins, but episode 3 flashes back to the strange interview that led to him landing the job.
body: Janus Cosmetics is the company owned by the wealthy Sionis family in DC Comics. Roman Sionis inherits the business after the death of his parents, but his disastrous tenure as its leader eventually leaves it on the brink of financial ruin. A product rushed to market without adequate testing disfigures hundreds of customers, forcing Roman to accept a bailout from Bruce Wayne and surrender control of the company.

Roman blames Bruce for this humiliation, and in seeking revenge, he becomes Black Mask, the Gotham City crime lord first introduced by Doug Moench and Tom Mandrake in 1985’s Batman #386. Janus is also the Roman god commonly depicted with two faces and associated with transitions, duality, beginnings, and endings. Naming the character “Roman” as a first name and associating him with a company called Janus is a pretty on-the-nose reference.

articles.title: This week in PC games: Bank Holiday Mawnday Edition
articles.summary: Fleeing the intolerable glare of another weekday morning, you take the spiral stair that runs around the elven bulk of the Treehouse, and after hours of climbing, reach the Primrose Door. The light within the Tree is soft as syrup, spilling across a realm of marble, gold, and glass.
body: There is no Ollie ambling amongst the shelves of blue and emerald books. No Julian rearranging the unidentifiable pieces on the war table. No James with his enamelled spanner, hunkered down beneath the great brass telescope. The guardians of the Treehouse have succumbed yet again to the siren song of Bank Holiday Monday. Deserting their duty, they carouse and bicker in the lands beyond the Tree, and in their absence, what dreams may come?

Across one wall of the instrument-crowded chamber, there is a huge and immaculate silver mirror. It gives back a perfect recreation of the room, and yourself within it. But there is one anomaly: a figure moves among the deeper shelves behind you. It is indistinct, a clot of feathery dull crimson. It is getting closer. Quickly, young one. You have brought new videogame releases to share, yes? Reach into your satchel, without moving your gaze from that hungry reflection. Present your prize. In the holiday absence of Rock Paper Shotgun's staff, it falls to you to FEED THE MAW. We'll be back properly tomorrow, assuming there is a Treehouse to return to.

articles.title: Steam Week in Review: Here are the top 10 most popular genres on Steam
articles.summary: All the interesting Steam facts for the week ending August 30.
body: A ridiculous amount of games release on Steam every week and basically none of them make any money. It only takes a cursory browse of Steam's unfiltered new release list to understand why this is true.

But which genre is most likely to make money or be a hit? Ichiro Lambe, Matt Martindale and Dr. Tim Ermilov have collaborated on a Steam revenue report on weloveit.io and, as the name implies, the purpose of the site is to estimate the earnings of all Steam games, or at least, those with a price tag and at least one review.

The trio doesn't have access to Valve's internal sales data, so they rely on the Boxleiter method to estimate that data, which assumes that a games' review count is "roughly proportional of its sales, so multiplying reviews by a constant gives an estimated unit count." For a standard estimate (rather than a conservative or generous one) the multiplier is 35 times the amount of user reviews.

articles.title: Activision sends a legal rep to a Call of Duty cheat seller's front door, films the whole thing, posts it online
articles.summary: Activision has posted footage of one of its legal representatives turning up at the Ohio home of a notorious Call of Duty cheat seller and handing over a cease-and-desist order.
body: The roughly one-minute clip went up on the official Call of Duty account on Friday, although the cease and desist was actually served on 22nd August, during last weekend's Modern Warfare 4 closed beta.
It shows a representative pulling up outside a house, meeting a man whose face is blurred throughout, and handing over paperwork.
"I just got some paperwork for you," he said. "Attorneys for Activision and, uh, it's a cease-and-desist order for you."
He tells the man to contact the attorney's office listed on the documents and leaves. No shouting, no chase, no drama – just papers served on a doorstep.
